svg.title: RSTP port roles and states drawn on a three-switch topology, showing the alternate port as a healthy link carrying nothing
svg.desc: Three switches: a root bridge above, two access switches below, each with a root port toward the root, and a link between them where one side is designated and the other is alternate and discarding. A comparison beside it lists the four roles, root, designated, alternate and backup, and the three states, discarding, learning and forwarding. A note explains that an alternate port is fully healthy and deliberately idle, and that the count of alternate ports is the bandwidth the design has paid for and not used, which is exactly what clustering exists to remove.
svg.text: Roles describe intent, states describe permission — and one of them means "healthy but forbidden"
The alternate port is the whole reason this chapter has a section on clustering
the dashed link is healthy, paid for, and discarding
it becomes forwarding the moment the root port dies
In a triangle, exactly one link per VLAN is wasted like this. Count them.
the best path toward the root, one per switch, forwarding
the best path toward the segment, one per segment, forwarding
another path to the root through a different switch, discarding
a second path to the same segment on the same switch, discarding
RSTP keeps alternate and backup ready, so the switchover needs no timer.
Backup is so rare that seeing one usually means hub or cabling duplication.
no learning, no forwarding — what a blocked port really is
building the MAC table without forwarding, a short lived state
learn and forward; only edge ports reach this without waiting
802.1D had five states. RSTP has three, and two of them are transient.
Every alternate port is a measurement: bandwidth you bought, powered up, monitored, and forbidden to carry traffic.
That count is the business case for clustering, and also its cost: clustering removes the idle port and replaces it with a peer link that must never be split.
Nothing in this chapter removes the trade — it only chooses where the failure lives: on the blocked link, or on the peer link.
